concept: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness

claims.text: CBT-I is a preferred behavioral approach to insomnia, but PD-specific efficacy and implementation should be described cautiously: the computerized ACCORD-PD trial showed better insomnia scores among completers, yet its intention-to-treat comparison was not significant and treatment dropout was high. (medium confidence)
Polysomnography is not routine for uncomplicated insomnia assessment, but can help when sleep-disordered breathing, RBD or other sleep-related movements may explain disturbed sleep. (low confidence)

NICE recommends considering modafinil for PD-related excessive daytime sleepiness only after a detailed sleep history excludes reversible drug-related and physical causes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

The cited review describes insomnia assessment as including a clinical sleep interview that checks medication effects, the sleep environment and comorbid sleep disorders; it notes that polysomnography is not routine for insomnia but may help when sleep-disordered breathing, RBD or other nocturnal movements are suspected. (low confidence)

NICE advises that PD patients with daytime sleepiness or sudden sleep onset avoid driving and consider occupational hazards, with specialist-guided medication adjustment. It advises considering modafinil only after a detailed sleep history excludes reversible medication-related and physical causes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

The ACCORD-PD pilot found greater insomnia improvement among computerized CBT-I completers than education completers, but not in intention-to-treat analysis; dropout in the CBT-I group was 43%. Adherence limits generalizability. (low confidence)

PD sleep complaints require separate assessment of insomnia, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and excessive daytime sleepiness; results on overall sleep quality should not be assumed to establish efficacy for each phenotype. (medium confidence)

The September 2026 phenotype-stratified meta-analysis concluded that pharmacological evidence for PD daytime sleepiness, insomnia and RBD remained insufficient for definitive recommendations; very high heterogeneity made pooled estimates for those domains exploratory. Improvement in overall sleep quality must not be substituted for proof of a specific sleep-disorder benefit. (low confidence)

NICE recommends considering clonazepam or melatonin for PD-related RBD after reviewing medication causes; the 2023 AASM guideline conditionally suggests clonazepam and specifically immediate-release melatonin for secondary RBD. These are conditional treatment options rather than proof that every formulation works. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

In a placebo-controlled trial of thirty people with PD-RBD, prolonged-release melatonin 4 mg did not reduce RBD events; the primary endpoint comparison was not significant (P = 0.92). This finding concerns that formulation and trial, rather than disproving all melatonin regimens. (low confidence)

A negative prolonged-release melatonin trial should not be presented as a test of immediate-release melatonin: in 30 PD patients, 4 mg prolonged-release melatonin over 8 weeks did not reduce RBD compared with placebo, while AASM separately conditionally recommends immediate-release melatonin and finds insufficient evidence for prolonged-release melatonin in secondary RBD. (medium confidence)

In the ACCORD-PD pilot, 28 participants were recruited; completion was 8/14 with computerized CBT-I versus 13/14 with standard education. Insomnia Severity Index improvement favored CBT-I among completers (−7.9 versus −3.5), but the intention-to-treat comparison was not significant (p = 0.48). (low confidence)

Modafinil is a conditional clinical option rather than a reliably effective treatment for every sleepy PD patient: NICE says to consider it after excluding reversible causes, but a placebo-controlled trial of 40 patients found no significant improvement in subjective Epworth sleepiness or objective multiple sleep latency testing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

RBD involves loss of REM muscle atonia with dream enactment and potential injury; a 2021 critical review describes clinical dream-enactment history plus video-polysomnographic confirmation as necessary for diagnosis. (low confidence)

The AASM recommends a safe RBD sleeping environment: remove weapons and dangerous bedside objects, pad or move sharp furniture, place a soft surface beside the bed, and consider separate sleeping for severe uncontrolled behaviors. (low confidence)

For secondary RBD, the AASM advises accounting for clonazepam-related sedation and imbalance, especially in older adults; reported adverse events include daytime sleepiness, dizziness and postural instability. (low confidence)

The 2020 PD insomnia review places CBT-I within the general first-line approach to insomnia while emphasizing that PD-specific randomized trials were small; general insomnia evidence should not be presented as large-trial PD-specific proof. (low confidence)

The 2019 MDS review rated melatonin and eszopiclone for PD insomnia as possibly useful despite insufficient efficacy evidence; these ratings should not be rewritten as established efficacy. (low confidence)

NICE advises people with PD who have daytime sleepiness or sudden sleep onset not to drive and to consider occupational hazards; medication adjustment should follow specialist advice. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

Modafinil evidence in PD is mixed: MDS 2019 calls it possibly useful while retaining insufficient efficacy evidence, and one placebo-controlled trial found no significant improvement in either Epworth scores or objective sleep latency. Response should not be assumed. (high confidence)

For PD patients with obstructive sleep apnea, the 2019 MDS review considered CPAP likely efficacious and possibly useful for improving sleep and daytime sleepiness; this evidence does not apply indiscriminately to all PD sleepiness. (low confidence)

The 2025 systematic review pooled pharmacological trials and reported improvements in insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness but no statistically significant pooled RBD benefit; certainty ranged from very low to moderate. This class-level pooling does not establish efficacy of every included drug. (low confidence)
RBD involves loss of normal REM muscle atonia and dream enactment that can injure the patient or bed partner. (medium confidence)

The cited sources note that clonazepam for RBD carries risks including morning sedation, gait imbalance or falls, cognitive adverse effects, and worsening sleep-disordered breathing; age and pre-existing imbalance affect selection and dosing. (low confidence)

The 2023 AASM guideline conditionally supports transdermal rivastigmine for PD-associated RBD, based on one randomized trial; reported adverse effects include hypotension, asthenia, daytime sleepiness and nausea. (low confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
narrative.text: The cited sources distinguish dream enactment with injury risk, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness in PD. The AASM guideline pairs environmental safety advice with conditional drug options for RBD; clonazepam and immediate-release melatonin have conditional guideline support, while prolonged-release melatonin failed in a small PD trial. Insomnia assessment considers other sleep disorders, and CBT-I evidence in PD is promising but limited by small studies and adherence. NICE describes a medication review, a search for reversible causes and driving precautions for daytime sleepiness. Modafinil has mixed efficacy evidence; CPAP evidence applies to coexisting obstructive sleep apnea. Guideline options and positive pooled findings should retain their evidence limitations.
